2. Nucleotide excision repair

A general theme that pervaded the workshop discussions is the remarkable overlap between enzymes required for excision repair and those needed in a number of other cellular transactions, most notably transcription, but also DNA replication, mitotic recombination and cell-cycle control. The dual roles of certain enzymes may be important to the regulation of the respective DNA transactions, but also in environmental stress situations the sharing of essential factors may result in competition for those in limiting supply. The most striking example of this dual functionality is the recently discovered implication of the multi-subunit transcription factor TFIIH in nucleotide excision repair (NER), as well as in RNA polymerase II transcription initiation. This has led to the notion, discussed in detail in Section 4.2 that the clinical features of some human hereditary diseases such as Cockayne Syndrome (CS) and trichothiodystrophy (TTD) may be understood as a malfunction of TFIIH in transcription rather than as a defect in its role in DNA repair.
2.1. NER in human cell extracts

NER has now been reconstituted in cell-free extracts and from assembled purified components. In human cells the complete mechanism involves over 25 polypeptides; this includes the basal transcription initiation factor TFIIH. Incision of UV-damaged or cis-platin-damaged DNA has been reconstituted with the purified proteins RPA, XPA, TFIIH (which includes XPB and XPD), XPC, XPG, ERCC1/XPF complex, and IF7 (Wood, ICRF, South Mimms). Wood also found that a type 2A protein phosphatase was required to optimize the repair reaction on UVdamaged DNA in vitro. It is likely that additional factors may participate in an auxiliary manner through their modulation of core component activities. The dual incisions in the damaged strand are introduced 3 to 9 phosphodiester bonds to the $3 ^ { \prime }$ side of the lesion by the XPG nuclease and 16 to 25 phosphodiester bonds to the $5 ^ { \prime }$ side of the lesion by the structure-specific ERCC1/XPF nuclease. It is now established that XPF, ERCC4, and ERCC11 represent the identical protein with the implication that ERCC4 and ERCC11 complementation is intragenic (Sijbers, Rotterdam and ICRF); This protein is homologous to Rad1 of S. cerevisiae, Rad16 of S. pombe and Mei-9 of Drosophila (Sijbers; also Thompson, Livermore), and it is able to cleave double-stranded DNA at the $5 ^ { \prime }$ side of a duplex singlestrand junction (de Laat et al., Rotterdam and ICRF). The complete repair replication reaction can be obtained if the incision factors are combined with RFC, PCNA, DNA polymerase epsilon (or delta) and DNA ligase I.

Considerable debate focused upon the question of whether the factors required for NER are pre-assembled in undamaged cells and whether they function in large aggregates termed repairosomes, or whether subsets of these factors are assembled as needed sequentially through the four basic operations required. These operations include: (1) lesion recognition; (2) incision and excision of the damaged stretch of DNA; (3) repair replication; and (4) ligation.
2.2. Protein—protein interactions

Using the cloned genes for TFIIH subunits (including XPB, XPD, p62, p44, and p34) as well as the cloned XPG, CSA and CSB genes, Friedberg and associates (Dallas) analyzed protein-protein interactions using co-immunoprecipitation of in vitro translated polypeptides and/or the yeast two-hybrid system. XPB, XPD, p44, and p62 proteins were found to interact with each other. XPG protein interacted with several subunits of TFIIH and also with CSB protein. CSA protein interacted with CSB and with p44. A yeast homologue of the CSA gene was cloned and designated RAD28. Rad28 mutants are viable and normally resistant to UV. Although Rad28 did not interact with Rad26, the yeast homologue of CSB, in the two-hybrid system, Rad28 did interact with human CSB protein and Rad26 interacted with CSA. Hanaoka and coworkers (Osaka) also obtained evidence for complex formation between XPG and TFIIH, using association of the purified proteins and also through their co-purification through several steps. In contrast, using functional, epitope tagged TFIIH Hoeijmakers (Rotterdam), in collaboration with Egly (Strasbourg), did not find stable associations of TFIIH with XPG or CSB in repair-competent extracts assayed under physiological conditions. CSA and CSB were found in separate large protein complexes of different sizes, and a further complex contained XPC and the bound fraction of hHR23B (see below), while ERCC1/XPF was largely free. These results are consistent with a model in which the repairosome may assemble at the site of a lesion, rather than operating as a preformed complex. The studies that implicate protein-protein interactions may be revealing the 'docking sites' for the eventual protein contacts during the coordinated sequence of steps in NER.

XP-C is of particular interest because it is one of the most common of the XP complementation groups, but also because it appears to control NER of global genome repair, with no involvement in the specialized transcription-coupled repair pathway (see Section 2). Hanaoka and coworkers have shown that the XPC gene product is tightly associated with one of the two human homologues of Rad23, namely hHR23B. In a reconstituted cell-free NER system recombinant XPC protein corrected an XPC defect only weakly but this activity was stimulated upon addition of recombinant hHR23B, suggesting a role for this protein in the global repair pathway.
2.3. Mechanisms of lesion recognition

Studies on the UvrABC system from E. coli continue to provide important mechanistic information. New results were presented on the mechanisms of DNA damage recognition and incision catalyzed by the UvrABC endonuclease from E. coli. Delagoutte et al. (Strasbourg) elaborated on factors determining the efficiency of incision of acetylaminofluorene (AAF) adducts residing at different G sequence positions within the NarI site (GGCGCC). They concluded that the UvrB-DNA complexes yielding efficient incision are much less stable than those formed with poorly inciseable DNA (i.e., AAF residing at the second G of the GGCGCC sequence). Footprints of the less stable UvrB-DNA complexes can only be visualized transiently at low temperature, whereas the $\mathrm { U v } \mathbf { \Lambda } \mathbf { A } _ { 2 } \mathbf { B }$ recognition complex is similarly formed with all DNA substrates. These results are consistent with a model in which dynamic flexibility of the UvrB-DNA complex as determined by the sequence context and type of lesion is essential for incision/excision efficiency. Van Houten et al. (Galveston) have studied in great detail the interactions of the UvrABC enzyme with all isoforms of modified $\aleph ^ { 2 }$ -guanine benzo(a)pyrene-diolepoxide (BPDE) adducts. For all substrates they found similar recognition efficiencies; however, incisions were more efficient at cisisomers and the $( + ) .$ -enantiomers of both the cisand the trans-isomers. Fluorescence spectroscopic analysis of the interaction of UvrA with BPDE-DNA suggested that hydrophobic interactions as well as phosphate charge interactions are important for damage recognition. Again, there was no correlation between recognition by UvrA and the incision efficiency by the UvrABC enzyme complex.

Protein-protein interactions between UvrB and UvrC proteins were studied by Moolenaar et al. (Leiden). Deletion of the C-terminal end of UvrB prevents its interaction with UvrC; however, this interaction is not essential for the $5 ^ { \prime }$ incision made by UvrC, nor is the UvrB C-terminal end essential for the $3 ^ { \prime }$ incision. They suggested that the short region of homology between UvrB and UvrC may constitute the sites involved in the protein-protein interactions. Results of mutagenesis studies led to doubts being raised about the previous conclusion that the $5 ^ { \prime }$ incision is made by UvrC and the $3 ^ { \prime }$ incision by UvrB, and they suggest instead that both incisions are made by UvrC or by a complex of UvrB and UvrC.

Further elaboration on the efficiency of NER for different types of substrates was made by Naegeli et al. (Zurich). These investigators have developed a competition assay in which repair synthesis catalyzed by human cell free extracts on DNA containing a single AAF adduct is measured after addition of different types of competing damaged plasmid DNA. It appears that different lesions are recognized with efficiencies differing by at least two orders of magnitude: AAF being a good substrate and 8- methoxypsoralen being a very poor determinant for damage recognition. Model studies of this type are likely to be important for evaluating the role of NER in vivo for handling different types of DNA damage.

Jones et al. (Swansea) presented data to suggest that, in S. cerevisiae, Rad14 is directly involved in damage recognition in yeast and that the zinc finger domain of Rad14 may determine specificity. A specific point mutation (rad14-2) in this domain prevents repair of pyrimidinc dimers, but not of pyrimidine hydrates (monitored as endonuclease-III-sensitive sites). A deletion mutant of RAD14 is, however, defective in repair not only of CPDs as expected, but also unexpectedly of pyrimidine hydrates, as are other mutants defective in NER. Other studies monitoring removal of thymine glycols with an antibody suggest, however, that base excision repair is important for repair of pyrimidine hydrates. This apparent discrepancy might be explained by endonuclease III monitoring a larger variety of DNA lesions than just pyrimidine hydrates.

Lombaerts et al. (Leiden) reported on the identification of a yeast gene with sequence similarity to XPE from mammalian cells. Interestingly, targeted disruption of this gene in yeast yielded a nonviable mutant as has been observed previously for RAD3. Further characterization is required to establish whether the yeast XPE homologue is yet another component of the NER machinery in yeast that also has an essential function.

The work of Yasui et al. (Sendai and Rotterdam) has provided evidence for the existence of a photolyase gene in human cells. The gene product shows homology to class I photolyases, which comprise most microbial photolyases. It is also similar to the plant blue light receptors. It remains to be analyzed by expression analysis whether the gene indeed expresses a protein with a photolyase function.

Pedrini et al. (Pavia) reported on the UV-induced interference of topoisomerase action. Topoisomerase I is apparently trapped within a DNA strand by UV-irradiation due to constraints in resolution of the DNA strands following swivelling. Such trapped intermediates may account for at least some of the protein-DNA cross-links formed by UV-irradiation.

DNA damage recognition is a crucial and complex element in all excision repair processes. Although in vitro studies may be interpreted such that recognition can occur by a specific type of repair system, the abundance and availability of different repair enzyme systems in vivo may be the determining consideration for how different types of damage are handled by different pathways in the cell.
2.4. NER in the yeasts, S. cerevisiae and S. pombe

The S. cerevisiae RAD16 gene is required for the repair by NER of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPD) in nontranscribed DNA. It is not yet clear whether the Rad16 protein is involved in lesion recognition or rather in permitting the NER complex access to CPD in such regions. The S. pombe homologue has been cloned (Bang et al., Leiden) and, as in S. cerevisiae, this gene is inducible. However, unlike in S. cerevisiae, its disruption does not confer UV sensitivity but it does confer cis-platinum sensitivity. This may be because of compensation by an alternative UV excision repair pathway in S. pombe (see below), although it should be borne in mind that disruption of genes essential for all NER generally confer considerable UV sensitivity in S. pombe. Why the alternative pathway should compensate much more for the repair of CPD in nontranscribed DNA is not known at present. No human homologue of this gene has yet been identified and the search continues (Bang et al.). A second role for RAD16 has been identified: enhanced NER of CPD is seen if cells receive a small UV dose before a second higher dose (compared to that seen after the second dose alone). This effect is absent in rad16 mutants. With respect to the expression of RAD16 in the mitotic cell cycle, the RAD16 mRNA is not degraded in Gl as in the other phases. Scott et al. (Swansea) examined the enhanced repair of CPD through the mitotic cell cycle. In synchronized populations it was restricted to G1- and possibly early S-phase, thus correlating with the enhanced stability of RAD16 mRNA. When cells were arrested at precise points in late Gl using cdc4 and cdc28 mutants, there was surprisingly no excision of CPD. Either the products of the CDC4 and CDC28 genes have a direct role in NER, or NER is prevented from operating in the late G1 state at which these cells arrest.

The roles of many S. cerevisiae NER products have been elucidated. Rad1 and Rad10 proteins (homologues of human XPF and ERCC1) are subunits of an endonuclease cleaving at the ${ \pmb 5 } ^ { \prime }$ side of DNA lesions. Monoclonal antibodies were used to identify two regions of Rad1 essential for cleavage and these inhibit NER in vitro (Tomkinson et al., San Antonio and Dallas). The Rad1 /Rad10 complex has no affinity for DNA damage and the recognition of damage is mediated by Radl4. However, in cells over-producing Rad14, affinity purification indicated that Rad14 co-purifies with Rad1 and Rad10 in the absence of DNA damage. This suggests that for NER, these three products may be pre-associated and either form part of a repairosome or part of a complex that contributes to the assembly of a repairosome at the site of damage. Whether Rad2, which incises at the $3 ^ { \prime }$ side of the lesion is also part of such a complex remains to be elucidated.

S. pombe also possesses an NER pathway and its Swi10 product, the homologue of Rad10 in S. cerevisiae and human ERCC1, is involved in both mating type switching and NER. Rodel and Schmidt (Braunschweig) analyzed the gene by site directed mutagenesis. The DNA binding motif has been identified and deletion of this motif abolishes both switching and NER. Both ERCCl and an N-terminal fragment of swil0 were able to complement the switching defect but not the UV sensitivity of the swil0 deletion strain. Apart from full-length swil0, only a chimaeric ERCCl (N-terminal)-swil0 (Cterminal) construct was able to complement the UV sensitivity.

Unlike S. cerevisiae, S. pombe has an additional alternative excision pathway for the repair of both CPD and 6-4 photoproducts which is distinct from NER (Yasui et al., Sendai; McCready et al., Oxford; Murray et al., Sussex). The alternative pathway entails the action of UVDE, an endonuclease which incises ${ \boldsymbol { 5 } } ^ { \prime }$ to these lesions and a short oligonucleotide is removed by Rad2 which is a ${ 5 ^ { \prime } } – 3 ^ { \prime }$ exonuclease or a flap endonuclease. Mutants in the two pathways exhibit distinct phenotypes: those for NER are more UV-sensitive than are those for the alternative pathway, despite more excision of CPD and 6-4 photoproducts occurring in the former. The genetic analysis of mutants for the alternative pathway has led to the generalizing proposal that UVDE-incised lesions may be processed by a number of routes: excision, recombination, error-prone repair and a possible pathway leading to cell death. The Rad12 protein has a role in a number of pathways: it possibly regulates
UVDE activity, but rad12 does not encode UVDE, contrary to a previous suggestion in the literature.

From these fungal systems it is evident that relationships exist between NER and a number of other cellular processes, such as recombination and cellcycle arrest. Clearly, the powerful genetic approaches available for these organisms will assist in unravelling the nature of these relationships.
2.5. Other proteins

Studies of NER in rodent cell lines belonging to several complementation groups sensitive to ionizing radiation and deficient in double-strand break repair have suggested that the Ku/DNA-dependent protein kinase may be involved in NER, but it is not yet clear which step(s) is affected (Salles et al., Toulouse).

Ackerman and his associates (Bethesda and Galveston) have characterized a highly efficient NER system in nuclear extracts of Xenopus as well as in the injected oocytes. Both the high efficiency and the DNA polymerase requirements appeared to be different from those implicated in mammalian cell extracts. Using polymerase-specific antibodies they showed that both DNA polymerases $\alpha$ and $\beta$ were required for repair of UV-induced photoproducts or AAF adducts.

We now probably know essentially all of the gene products required to carry out the process of NER. What we still do not know for sure is the sequence in which these proteins and complexes (such as TFIIH) operate. There is good evidence that XPG cuts the damaged strand first on the $3 ^ { \prime }$ side of the lesion, followed by XPF/ERCCl cutting on the $5 ^ { \prime }$ side. However, it is not yet established whether TFIIH (containing helicases XPB and XPD) really is involved in opening up the damaged duplex DNA prior to cutting or whether it operates in the removal of the damaged segment following incision. (In $E .$ coli, by possible analogy, the UvrD helicase appears to operate at this later step.) We also do not know unambiguously which protein associations are preformed and which occur through the course of the NER sequence. The next major advances in the NER field should answer these questions as well as those relating to the localization of NER reactions in the intact cell.
. Gene-specific repair
3.1. CS and XP-C (see also Section 4)

The most prominent example of intragenomic heterogeneity of repair, now usually termed transcription coupled repair (TCR) is the increased rate or extent of removal of certain lesions from the transcribed strands of active genes, observed in bacteria, yeast and mammalian cells. The apparent lack of this process in CS-A and CS-B cells, and its persistence in XP-C cells, led to the notion that TCR and so-called 'global' repair are distinct processes. The stalling of transcription at a lesion would recruit the actual excision/resynthesis machinery to the lesion via CS proteins, while another system, deficient in XP-C, would facilitate detection in the rest of the genome by overcoming barriers posed by packing of DNA into chromatin. However, the recent demonstration of the involvement of TFIIH in both transcription and the actual excision steps in NER, the association of CS with mutations in genes clearly involved directly in both TFIIH and excision nuclease functions, and the finding that elements of the mismatch repair system have roles in TCR argue strongly against such a simple view. Although attempts to elucidate the mechanism of TCR by studies in vitro are now beginning, most of the presentations concerned studies of removal of a variety of different lesions in diverse cell types and characterized mutants, many of which were in yeast systems.

Spivak et al. (Stanford and ICRF) described attempts to develop a repair system using cell extracts that would exhibit TCR. Comparisons of repair in fragments containing either expressed or silent lacZ genes, present simultaneously on different plasmids under conditions allowing transcription, did not demonstrate any preference for the lesions in the template of the active gene. They ascribe this to inefficient transcription combined with efficient repair, and are now attempting to isolate those plasmids supporting transcription prior to analysis of repair.

The underlying basis for the complex nature of the defect in CS cells was an important theme at the meeting and is discussed in detail in Section 4. One model proposes that the clinical symptoms of CS result from a deficiency in the rapid and efficient

TCR of endogenous, probably oxidative damage in some critical genes during development. Some time ago, such a form of TCR after ionizing radiation was shown to be present in repair-proficient cells and NER-deficient XP-A cells but absent in CS-A and CS-B cells, which are deficient in TCR of CPD. This model must somehow account for an impact on this process by those mutations in XPB, XPD and XPG genes that result in CS. An involvement of XPG in this process was the subject of work by Cooper et al. (Berkeley, Geneva and Chapel Hill), who examined metallothionein genes for repair of ionizing radiation damage, and for removal of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ induced thymine glycols. XP-G cells from patients showing severe XP symptoms but not CS involvement exhibited TCR but it was significantly delayed compared to the response in normal or XP-F cells, and overall repair was less efficient. In XP-G cells from patients with CS symptoms, the TCR was absent, and the overall repair was even more deficient. All the XP-G cells and the XP-F cells are severely deficient in NER, so these results suggest that an XP-G activity separate from its role in the incision step in NER is required for TCR of oxidative damage and lack of this process contributes significantly to the symptoms of CS. The linkage between this repair deficiency and the actual symptoms of CS is at present as mysterious as the proposed transcription defect discussed in Section 4.

A detailed comparative analysis of the response of normal, XP-C. CS-A and CS-B cells to UV photoproducts (CPDs and 6-4 photoproducts), dG-C8-AF and dG-C8-AAF was presented by Mullenders (Leiden) and suggested a new model for the nature of the demonstrated defect in TCR mediated by NER in the CS-A and CS-B cells. In XP-C cells TCR is the only mechanism able to operate on all these lesions; however, in repair-proficient cells, neither the 6-4 photoproducts nor the aminofluorene lesions exhibited TCR, defined by the usual diagnostic, namely more rapid repair of the template DNA strand than its complementary strand. A likely explanation is that the efficiency of the global repair system is so high for these adducts that TCR is masked. CS cells are hypersensitive to killing by N-acetoxy-AAF but have no deficiency in the repair of AF adducts in active or inactive genes. Nevertheless RNA synthesis, inhibited by such treatments, fails to recover, a response resembling that observed after UV-irradiation. This suggests that the sensitivity of CS cells to such lesions may be the result of a direct defect in recovery of RNA synthesis rather than an inability to target lesions in genes for efficient repair. A model that might account for these observations is that DNA damage stimulates the commitment of TFIIH complexes to repair activity, and the CS factors are involved in restoring TFIIH to its role in transcription initiation following repair. The lack of TCR of CPD in CS cells would be an indirect result of the sudden down-regulation of the genes examined.
3.2. Yeast systems

TCR and its relation to global genomic repair in yeast was discussed by Brouwer (Leiden). In the following, it should be kept in mind that 'repair' refers only to removal of CPD while survival was (necessarily) measured after introduction of all photoproducts induced by UV. The homolog of CSB, Rad26, is necessary for efficient TCR in yeast, but there is a some residual TCR of both the RPB2 and GAL7 genes (dependent upon ongoing transcription), and rad26 mutants are not UV sensitive. Like XPC in humans, RAD16 and RAD7 are both required for repair of inactive DNA; neither gene is however the homologue of XPC. Single rad16 or rad7 mutants are UV sensitive, to the same degree as the double mutants; however, when either single or the double mutant is combined with rad26, UV sensitivity is increased dramatically, but still not to the level of a rad2 mutant, completely deficient in incision. This suggests that the global repair system can repair UV damage efficiently enough to prevent hypersensitivity to UV, and that unrepaired damage both within and outside transcription templates contribute significantly to cell killing. Presumably some lesions can be repaired by RAD2-dependent NER in the absence of these three factors; if they all function to give repair systems access to lesions, perhaps some subset of lesions are already accessible or can be made so by proteins with roles in other processes. TFIIS and Rad28 (the homolog of CSA) do not appear to be fulfilling this role, judged by studies with appropriate mutants.

The recent demonstration of defective TCR in bacterial and human tumour cells mutant in mismatch repair genes suggests they might be involved, but extensive studies with yeast mutants by Sweder et al. (Piscataway, Stanford, Leiden and Atlanta) failed to show any involvement of these proteins in TCR. This was true for msh2 mutants even when in combination with rad7, rad26, or both. For ribosomal DNA (Verhage et al., Leiden), transcribed by a different polymerase and existing in a form that appears to be non-nucleosomal when active, both strands were repaired efficiently, even in rad26 mutants, with the transcribed strand perhaps slightly faster. In rad7 and rad16 mutants the repair of the non-transcribed strand is reduced to $50 \%$ roughly the fraction of inactive, nucleosomal ribosomal DNA sequences. In mutants in rad4, the homologue of XPC, the repair of the non-transcribed strand was abolished, leaving about $50 \%$ repair of the transcribed strand. Rad4 mutants are almost completely deficient in overall repair, suggesting that a stalled RNA PolI on ribosomal DNA substitutes for the functions provided by rad26, rad4 and rad7 / 16 required in a location-specific manner at other CPDs.

Mueller and Smerdon (Pullman) showed that the repair deficiency of rad7 mutants characterized for the genome also occurs with a plasmid system; most of the repair occurred in transcribed sequences. Repair of the genome overall in rad23 mutants was shown to be about as deficient as in rad7 mutants. Rad23 protein forms a complex with Rad4 protein and one of the Rad23 homologues in mammalian cells forms a complex with XPC protein. However. the deficiency in rad23 mutants is not as severe as for rad4. Repair in the RPB2 gene both on a plasmid and in the genome in rad23 was only about $1 5 \%$ .The homology between Rad16 and Snf2 provides support for the notion that requirement for Rad16 in repair of silent sequences relates to modulation of the binding of chromatin proteins to DNA (See Section 3.3).
3.3. Repair at the nucleotide level

Holmquist (Duarte) discussed excision repair at the level of the individual nucleotide in human cells. He reviewed the data showing that for the $P G K I$ and JUN genes, CPD are removed much faster from the sites on transcribed strands than from non-transcribed strands, but that this property does not always start at the same point along the DNA. It begins at roughly 140 bases downstream from transcription start in PGK1, while in JUN it starts 40 bases upstream. TCR is less apparent in JUN, possibly because the repair of the non-transcribed strand is more rapid. In promoters, repair rates can vary widely, as can induction rates, and strand specificity is not observed. Studies of the repair of methylpurines formed by dimethylsulphate confirmed the lack of strand bias observed several years ago for CHO cells at kilobase resolution. Adducts to adenine were repaired faster than those to guanine. Repair rates among the sites were variable, but no sequence context was apparent. When repair was carried out in vitro using purified glycosylase, rates of removal varied at different sites, but did not correlate with the rates found in cells. Tijsterman et al. (Leiden) studied repair kinetics at the nucleotide level in the RPB2 gene of yeast, and found results similar to those in human cells: relatively uniform rates of removal in the transcribed sequence, with faster repair in the transcribed strand, and highly variable repair in the promoter region. The repair in the gene itself in rad7, rad16 and rad26 mutants was consistent with studies of repair at low resolution, but in the promoter, complex variations in the mutants was observed, in a site-specific manner. Reed et al. (Swansea) studied repair at the nucleotide level in the 300 bp mfa2 gene of yeast, which is silent in mating type-a cells, and active in $\alpha$ cells. The small size of this gene and some modifications of the end-labelling method used greatly facilitates the analysis. The expected behaviour of normal cells was observed: relatively uniform repair rates along the reading frame and faster repair in the transcribed strand only when transcription was active.

McGregor et al. and Wei et al. (East Lansing) carried out extensive studies of repair in the HPRT gene in human fibroblasts. Using ligase-mediated PCR. they compared the rate of removal of 1-nitrosopyrene (NOP) and BPDE adducts at specific guanine sites in exon 3 of HPRT. Overall, 1-NOP adducts were removed 2-3 times faster than BPDE adducts, but the fine structure of differences in rate between sites was not the same for the two lesions, suggesting that the rate at a particular site depends both on sequence context and the actual lesion being recognized and removed. They also compared repair for these two adducts and those (almost exclusively dG-C8-AF) formed by treatment with NA-AAF at the gene level of resolution, using UvrABC nuclease to cleave at sites of lesions. When cells were treated with doses resulting in $3 7 \%$ cell survival (8 BPDE, 25 1-NOP, 50 AF adducts per million nucleotides) mutation frequencies were 160, 80 and 40 per million cells. Repair of 1-NOP adducts was about 2.5 times faster than repair of BPDE adducts, and both showed moderate strand specificity; however, repair of the dG-C8-AF adducts was even slower than that of BPDE, and showed no strand bias, similar to the result mentioned above. In vitro, BPDE adducts blocked transcription by the phage T7 RNA polymerase about 4 times better than the other two adducts. Thus the repair rates do not provide a simple explanation of the mutagenicity data. It should be kept in mind that cell killing may significantly reflect induction of some apoptotic process, which may not be directly related to lesion frequency or repair rates, and that minor adducts may contribute to mutagenicity.
3.4. New methodology

Van Houten et al. (Galveston) presented successful development of a gene-specific repair assay in which PCR of up to $1 8 \ \mathrm { k b }$ was sufficiently quantitative for calculation of the frequency of lesions due to their blocking the polymerase. Repair in the HPRT gene of UV-irradiated human cells was much faster than repair in the inactive region encompassing the $\beta$ -globin genes, and little or no repair was apparent in XP-A cells. Repair in a lymphoblastoid line appeared faster than in SV40 transformed fibroblasts and repair in the mismatch repair defective P2 line was slower than in a proficient cell. This assay measures the aggregate removal of all blocking lesions, which of course may be processed at different rates. Single-strand breaks and thymine glycols induced by hydrogen peroxide were also detectable; mitochondrial DNA suffered about threefold more damage with this agent than nuclear DNA, and mtDNA was poorly repaired. This assay requires very little material and should facilitate studies with tissue. As yet, it is not capable of examining individual strands.
3.5. Repair of different adducts in different genes

Besides the detailed mechanism for TCR we also seek to know the adducts and repair systems for which repair heterogeneity occurs and the biological consequences of such. Many presentations reflected studies with new genes, cell systems and adducts and the results are summarised in Table 1. There were two reports of attempts to measure gene-specific repair in specially constructed MEL and ES cell lines being thwarted by massive apoptotic responses (Vreeswijk et al., Leiden: van Sloun et al., Leiden).
3.6. Strand-specific repair and mutation

Jansen et al. (Leiden) investigated the mutational spectrum induced by the ethylating agents $N .$ -ethyl$N .$ -nitrosourea (ENU) and ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) in the HPRT gene of the excision repair deficient CHO cell line UV5 and in its parental cell line AA8. Mutation induction by ENU was 1.5 times higher in UV5 compared to AA8, while mutation induction by EMS was the same in both cell lines. The spectrum of ENU showed a fairly large fraction of AT to TA transversions in both cell lines while this type of mutations was absent in the EMS spectrum. Interestingly. in AA8 cells all AT to TA transversions were found at positions where the mutated $\mathrm { T }$ was located in the non-transcribed strand of the HPRT gene. This contrasts with the situation in UV5 where $30 \%$ of the mutated T's involved in AT to TA transversions were located in the transcribed strand. Since these types of mutations are most likely caused by mispairing of $\mathrm { O } ^ { 2 }$ -ethylthymine with thymine, the data suggest that in AA8 cells ${ \mathrm { O } } ^ { 2 }$ ethylthymine is specifically removed from the transcribed strand by NER. Both ethylating agents induce GC to AT transitions. Based on the division of mutated G's over the two strands, these data suggest that for EMS-induced mutations, most of the GC to AT transitions are caused by mispairing of $\mathrm { O } ^ { 6 }$ -ethylguanine with thymine, but that in the spectrum of ENU induced mutations part of the GC to AT transitions are caused by mispairing of $\mathrm { O } ^ { 2 }$ -ethylcytosine. A comparison of these mutations in UV5 and AA8 cells also suggests that $0 ^ { 2 }$ -ethylcytosine is preferentially removed from the transcribed strand of the HPRT gene by NER.
