text: 4. DNA repair and nuclear structures
The transcriptional status of the DNA is only one aspect of chromatin structure that may modulate
DNA repair. Several groups are investigating other aspects.
4.1. DNA damage / repair and the structural hierarchy of chromatin

At the nucleosome level, Schieferstein and Thoma (Zürich) examined UV-induced CPDs in a definedsequence nucleosome, reconstituted on a fragment of the yeast DED1 promoter containing a 40 bp stretch of five T-tracts. They found that CPDs are strongly modulated by nucleosome structure and the distribution differs from that found for mixed sequence nucleosomes. Although CPDs changed the rotational setting of DNA when nucleosomes were assembled onto pre-irradiated DNA, there was no effect of CPDs on the rotational setting of DNA irradiated after nucleosome formation. Nucleosome structure modulates repair of CPDs by photolyase. Sites in nuclease-sensitive DNA (e.g., nucleosome linkers and gene promoters) are removed within $1 5 ~ \mathrm { \ m i n }$ whereas sites in nucleosome cores take more than 2 h.
4.2. DNA repair at the nuclear matrix, or putative chromatin loop attachment sites in nuclei

Balajee et al. (Baltimore) used an immunological approach to identify DNA repair, replication and transcription sites in single nuclei. Very early repair occurred primarily in the nuclear matrix fraction (as compared to the chromatin loop fraction) in close association with transcription sites in hamster cells. The matrix fraction was found to be enriched in various repair-associated proteins (e.g., PCNA), and rcduced in basal transcription in CS cells (lacking TCR). Koehler and Hanawalt (Stanford) find there is an increase in CPD-containing DNA in the matrix fraction during the first hour after UV-irradiation in normal Chinese hamster ovary cells but not in an ERCC1 deficient mutant. This suggests there is a 'recruitment' of transcribed and nontranscribed DNA containing CPDs, to the matrix immediately after irradiation. The structure of the nuclear matrix is still somewhat ill-defined, and more information needs to be obtained relating the biochemical fractionations to actual structures in vivo.

A third form of structural hierarchy examined was the interstitial telomeric repeat sequences (ITRS) in Chinese hamster cells (Slijepcevic et al., Leiden). Four immortalized cell lines showed far more radiation-induced chromosome breaks in ITRS and telomerase activity than the non-transformed, primary hamster cells, suggesting a possible link between chromosome breaks in ITRS-containing regions of chromatin and telomerase activity.

A fourth structural category in nuclei is simply defined as heterochromatin, or very condensed chromatin containing primarily highly repetitive DNA. Surrallés et al. (Leiden) used molecular cytogenetic techniques to investigate the level of DNA repair in the heterochromatin region of chromosome 1 in human, and found a very low level of spontaneous and EMS-induced breaks in this region, even though a high level of repair occurred in the genome overall.
4.3. Modulation of chromatin structure during DNA repair

Peterson (Worcester) discussed the modulation of nucleosome structure by the SWI/SNF family of DNA-dependent ATPases in yeast. Despitc thc presence of helicase domains in this family, no helicase activity has been detected in any of the family members studied. Sub-families of this class of complexes include Rad5, Rad16 and Rad54 of S. cerevisiae, Rad8 of S. pombe and CSB (ERCC6) in mammalian cells. Peterson proposed that these proteins were involved in chromosome remodelling during repair of different types of damage.

Almouzni and coworkers (Paris and Cold Spring Harbor) examined chromatin assembly in Xenopus oocytes, and extracts of Xenopus eggs and human cells. Two chromatin assembly pathways are observed in injected oocytes, independent or dependent on DNA synthesis. Injection of UV-irradiated plasmids into oocytes yields specific DNA synthesis on these templates coupled to chromatin assembly. With extracts. the authors observe NER with plasmids irradiated with UVC or containing a single cisplatinum lesion. Coupled to the NER in vitro, is assembly of the repaired plasmids into nucleosomes, which requires chromatin assembly factor-1 (CAF-1) in the human cytosolic extract.

Solovjeva et al. (St. Petersberg, Quebec, Brighton, and Rotterdam) used monoclonal antibodies to localize XPB (ERCC3) and PCNA in UV-irradiated human cells. After UV-irradiation, PCNA rapidly accumulates in nuclei of non-S-phase cells as does XPB, but confocal analysis indicates that many of the XPB- and PCNA-associated granules are not associated. Furthermore, PCNA-containing complexes were detected in the nuclei of XP-A cells, indicating that these complexes are not solely associated with DNA repair synthesis. The results indicate that PCNA has a second, repair synthesis-independent, function in NER. In another study, Czibula et al. (Szeged, Hungary, Cambridge and Manchester) examined the proficiency of NER, alkylation damage repair and double-strand break (DSB) repair in mouse embryonic cells induced to differentiate. Undifferentiated cells removed UV-induced CPDs very rapidly, whereas a much more reduced NER capacity was observed in the differentiated state. Although no difference was observed in the first step of base excision repair (BER) between undifferentiated and differentiated cells, the latter cells show a decline in $\boldsymbol { 0 } ^ { 6 }$ -alkylguanine-DNA-alkyltransferase (ATase) activity. even when human ATase was injected into the cells. Lastly, both broken chromosomes and exchanges are observed following induction of DSBs.
5. Syndromes and animal models associated with defects in repair of UV damage
5.1. The cellular responses to DNA damage

To understand the genetic predisposition to skin cancer in repair-deficient syndromes, Abrahams et al. (Leiden) studied the induction of the SOS-like responses, Enhanced Reactivation (ER) and Enhanced Mutagenesis (EM), in UVC-irradiated skin fibroblasts from normal individuals, XP, and different cancer-prone patients. Previously, they reported that fibroblasts from XP patients which remain cancer-free in sun-exposed areas of the skin do not display ER. Here they showed that the ability to display an ER response is an hereditary trait and that the same cell lines which fail to show ER, also do not show the UV-induced expression of a protooncogene, ornithine decarboxylase (Terleth et al., Leiden).

There were several studies on DNA repair capacity in normal individuals and patients with different disorders. Abrahams et al. (Leiden) showed that repair capacity measured by Host-cell reactivation (HCR) of UVC-irradiated Herpes Simplex virus type 1(HSV-1) is lower in various hereditary cancer-prone syndromes. Repair of UV-induced photoproducts and their biological consequences were studied in different human syndromes deficient in nucleotide excision repair (NER). Clingen et al. (MRC, Brighton) (IIB.10) showed that UVB and UVC induce CPDs. (6-4) photoproducts, and Dewar isomers with markedly different proportions, and that (6-4) photoproducts are most effective for cell killing, and inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis.

The role of CPD and 6-4 photoproduct repair in cancer prevention in TTD patients was discussed by Mezzina et al. (Villejuif). They showed that in photosensitive TTD patients repair of CPDs is defective, whereas repair of 6-4 photoproducts both in active genes, as well as in the overall genome, is similar to that observed in cells from normal individuals. However, these data are not in agreement with the results obtained by the Brighton group but the reason for the observed discrepancy is not known.

Arlett et al. (MRC, Brighton) examined ionizing radiation sensitivity of several XP cell lines (23 cell lines) from various complementation groups. Three cell lines from group XP-C, D, and G displayed an increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation. An extreme $\mathbf { X }$ -ray sensitivity, similar to that in A-T patients, was found in XP14BR cells (XP-C). Transfection of the XPC gene restored only the UV but not the X-ray sensitivity, indicating that a separate novel gene involved in the cellular response to ionizing radiation is likely to be mutated in XPl4BR cells. The reason for the observed X-ray sensitivity in other XP cell lines is unknown, but it could be due to the variability of $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { X } }$ -ray sensitivity which is also observed in normal individuals. These studies indicate the importance of verification of radiosensitivity of XP. as well as other patients in case of any possible radiotherapy.
5.2. Transcription syndromes and mutation analysis in TFIIH related syndromes

DNA repair defects in XP complementation groups B and D are associated with the clinical features of the three quite different disorders; XP (sun-sensitive and cancer-prone), TTD or CS (multisystem disorders with no skin cancer). The finding of additional combined XP/CS patients falling in group B, D and G indicates that there is considerable overlap and clinical heterogeneity within a subset of complementation groups. To date most repair-deficient TTD cell strains have been assigned to XP group D, with the exception of TTD1BR (TTD-A) and TTD6VI and TTD4VI (XP group B).

The discovery that the XPB and XPD DNA repair helicases are involved in basal transcription and nucleotide excision repair has been extremely helpful in our understanding of clinical disorders associated with DNA repair defects. In view of this dual functionality of TFIIH it was postulated that a mutation in a subunit can affect either one or both of its functions. Classical XP may result from an impairment in the DNA repair function, whereas TTD and CS could be due to a crippled TFIIH, affecting the expression of certain genes or the stability of TFIIH. This also provides a rationale for the category of TTD and CS patients without NER defects. These non-photosensitive patients are hypothesised to harbour mutations that only affect the transcription function of TFIIH. At the same time this accounts for the extreme rarity of these syndromes in general. The relative abundance of XP-D can be explained by the fact that the gene can tolerate many mutations, because its helicase activity is not essential. The physical presence of XPD is more important for TFIIH than its functional integrity (J.H.J. Hoeijmakers). The finding by several laboratories of distinct mutations in the XPD gene associated with the disorders support this hypothesis (Lehmann).

These disorders caused by subtle disturbances of basal transcription were suggested to be part of a larger clinical spectrum reflecting transcription syndromes. Extensive genetic analysis using SSCP, REF and automatic sequencing of 31 patients considered to be candidates for such transcription syndromes but with normal UV sensitivity showed no involvement in the XPD gene, suggesting that viable mutations in this gene are most likely to cause UV sensitivity (Jaspers et al., Rotterdam)

Circumstantial evidence supports the idea that the transcription proteins p62, p44, p55 and p34 are also implicated in NER. This suggests that most if not all components of the transcription machinery participate in NER. It is possible that the TTDA protein (not cloned) is identical to the $\mathsf { p } 4 4$ TFIIH subunit. Recently, it became clear that in man this gene was duplicated during evolution. Both telomeric and centromeric gene copies are expressed and three amino acid differences were detected. Alternatively, the TTDA factor might have a tendency to (partly) dissociate during purification of TFIIH and may represent a new TFIIH subunit (Egly, Strasbourg).

Most important from the viewpoint of tumour aetiology are the observations that neither TTD nor CS patients have skin tumours nor severe skin pigmentation alterations, whereas most XP patients develop skin cancer during their lifespan. In the past there were lines of evidence supporting the hypothesis that impaired immunological surveillance was involved in the aetiology of skin cancer. Recent interesting findings from Krutmann and coworkers presented by Lehmann showed that ICAM1 expression was more severely reduced by UVB light in XP-D cells compared to wild-type or TTD cells.

In order to understand how different phenotypes can arise from mutations in the same gene, several labs (Stefanini et al., Pavia, Lehmann et al.. and Weber et al., Livermore) have identified a large number of XPD mutations (most are compound heterozygotes) in XP, TTD and $\tt X P / C S$ Although mutation analysis has not revealed obvious TTD or XP-specific domains within the XPD gene, one mutation is found $( \mathrm { A r g 6 8 3 T r p } )$ which is present in $70 \%$ of the XP-D patients analyzed. Two TTD specific mutations have been commonly found $( \mathrm { A r g } 7 2 2 \mathrm { T r p } )$ and (Arg1 12His).

Two labs (Stefanini, Pavia and Slor, Tel-Aviv) described a patient from Israel, which showed the cellular phenotype of CS (normal UDS and inability to recover normal RNA synthesis after UV), but no typical CS clinical features other than sun-sensitivity. Complementation was observed with CS-A and CS-B cells, so that this cell line represents a new complementation group.

The involvement of TFIIH in both transcription and repair, and the fact that some patients with the clinical features of both CS and XP have mutations in the XPD or XPB gene led to the suggestion that the symptoms of CS might result from some subtle defect in the transcriptional role of TFIIH. To explain the origin of the CS symptoms in patients with defects in the CSA, CSB, and XPG genes, none of which are essential genes, the model in its simple form suggests that these proteins can also have a direct involvement with transcription. A direct interaction of CSB protein with the transcription apparatus, for example, could advance this idea. The evidence for and against such interactions is discussed in Section 1.2.

Friedberg (Dallas) reported that the transcriptional activity of partially fractionated cell extracts was severely depressed in XP-B, XP-D, CS-A and CS-B cells. Since intact cells clearly could not sustain such a dramatic reduction in transcription, the interpretation of these interesting findings remains unclear at present. In contrast to these findings, immunodepletion of the CSB protein from cell extracts was found by van Gool et al. (Rotterdam) to have no effect on transcription or repair.

As discussed in Section 2.1, work of Cooper (Berkeley) and the lab of Clarkson (Geneva) showed that severely affected XPG/CS patients have reduced ability to remove thymine glycols. This suggests that defective transcription coupled repair of endogenous oxidative base damage may contribute to the clinical manifestations of CS in XP-G. The subtle mutation found in XP125L0 and XP124LO (mutation in the putative endonuclease active site) results in mild cutaneous abnormalities (without CS phenotype) and normal repair of thymine glycols. These observations are in agreement with the hypothesis that mutations which give rise to the CS phenotype might disrupt interactions with XPG that are important for transcription coupled removal of oxidative base damage.
5.3. Gene-targeted mice

Gene targeting is used to understand gene function in a whole-animal system—the mouse—and to model human inherited disease. The first genetargeted mouse with a DNA repair gene (ERCCl) deficiency was reported in 1993. In 1995, knockouts for XPA and XPC were reported. At this meeting additional information on the existing knockouts was presented and a number of new knockouts were reported.
5.3.1. Conventional knockouts

Most of the DNA repair gene targeting to date has involved the production of conventional gene knockouts, typically involving neo-gene insertion into the target locus, sometimes also generating a small deletion in the target gene, or a premature stop codon.

5.3.1.I. XPA. XPA knockouts (de Vries et al., Bilthoven and Utrecht) showed increased susceptibility to tumour induction by UV-B. A daily low dose of UV-B led to hyperkeratosis and ocular abnormalities, with a large increase in the frequency of skin tumours compared to controls. Benzo(a)pyrene administration. causing a bulky DNA lesion normally repaired by NER, led to an increase in internal tumours and an increased mutation rate in somatic cells (assayed by crossing a lacZ transgene into the XPA background) compared to wild-type controls.

The HPRT mutation frequency in somatic cells from XPA mice has also been studied (Bol et al., Leiden). Benzo(a)pyrene induced mutations in T cells from XPA knockout mice more rapidly than in controls. The second mutagen used, N-hydroxylAAF. which also generates lesions repaired by NER, failed to induce T-cell mutations in either genotype, probably because it failed to reach the spleen in its active form.

Fibroblasts isolated from XPA knockout mice (Frosina et al.. Genoa and Bilthoven; poster IIIB.19) were UV sensitive, with reduced UDS compared to controls. The mutant cells were easily immortalised, at which point they became less UV-sensitive. The significance of this observation was discussed in the context of the possibility that it might indicate the activation of an alternative repair pathway, or of a damage-tolerance mechanism.

5.3.1.2. CSB (ERCC6). CSB knockouts (van der Horst et al., Rotterdam) mimicking the mutation in the CS patient CS1AN were reported. This mutation introduces a stop codon into exon 5. Knockout mice were sensitive to UV-B, developing erythema at lower doses than control animals. Mutant mice were slightly smaller than controls, but did not exhibit other characteristic features of CS, such as infertility or severe neurological abnormalities. However, a significant decrease in locomotor activity and a tendency to waltz (a possible indication of a hearing problem), provided a preliminary indication of possible neurological changes in the knockout animals. Primary embryonic fibroblasts isolated from knockout embryos showed the characteristic cellular phenotype of CS: UV sensitivity. normal UDS, failure to recover RNA synthesis following UV and loss of preferential repair of the template strand of activelytranscribed genes. However, contrary to the situation in CS, CSB knockout mice showed preliminary indications of increased cancer incidence following either UV-B or DMBA treatments. $X P C / C S B$ double nulls were severely runted, with a disturbed gait, and died 20 days after birth.

5.3.1.3. ERCC1 (Donker et al., Rotterdam). Both a complete knockout and a deletion of the C-terminal seven amino acids were discussed. Both showed a severe growth defect with the complete knockout mice dying before 3 weeks of age and the C-terminal deletion mice dying before 6 months. Both types of mouse showed polyploidy and chromatin abnormalities in liver and kidney, ferritin deposition in spleen and lack of subcutaneous fat. It was suggested that, as with the previously-reported ERCCl knockouts, animals died of liver failure. The premature ageing observed in these animals could be due to a combination of NER and recombination defects ( ERCCl is homologous to RADl0 in S. cerevisiae, which is involved in mitotic recombination).

5.3.1.4. XPB. XPB knockouts (Donker et al., Rotterdam), mimicking the mutation found in the XP-B/CS patient XP11BE, were embryonic lethals, confirming an essential role for XPB as a component of the RNA polymerase II basal transcription factor TFIIH.

5.3.1.5. MHR6A and 6B (Roest et al., Rotterdam). S. cerevisiae rad6 mutants show increased sensitivity to UV, X-rays and alkylating agents and sporulation is affected. Primary embryonic fibroblasts derived from knockout mice for either of the mouse RAD6 homologues, MHR6A and $\it 6 B$ , were not UV-sensitive. MHR6A knockouts were normal, apart from reduced fertility in females. In the MHR6B knockouts, the males were sterile with defective spermatogenesis, leading to the suggestion that MHR6B could be involved in chromatin remodelling during spermatogenesis. Embryos homozygous for both MHR6A and $\boldsymbol { \epsilon } \boldsymbol { B }$ mutations failed to develop to E13.5.
5.3.2. Subtle gene alterations

Conventional knockouts cannot be used to introduce subtle gene mutations. One example where such mutations are essential is to study the relationship between XPD mutations and the resulting disease, which can be XP, XP/CS or TTD. The XP8BR mutation (causing XP/CS) has been introduced into the mouse XPD gene by double-replacement genetargeting in HPRT-deficient embryonic stem cells (de Boer et al., Rotterdam). In the first targeting step, part of the $3 ^ { \prime }$ end of the gene is deleted and replaced by a cassette containing neo-and hprt-markers. In the second targeting step, the markers are themselves replaced by a modified $3 ^ { \prime }$ end of the XPD gene, carrying the XP8BR mutation. An alternative strategy has also been used to introduce the TTD1BEL mutation (causing TTD). Here, in a single step, the $3 ^ { \prime }$ end of the mouse XPD gene has been replaced with an altered sequence containing a human cDNA-derived part of exon 22 containing the TTD1BEL mutation, globin gene splicing signals and a neo-gene inserted downstream. The phenotype of any mice arising from these targeted ES cells is eagerly awaited.
6. Mismatch repair and base excision repair
6.1. Mismatch repair

Drummond (Duke University) reviewed briefly the current situation regarding mismatch repair in mammalian cells and described a bidirectional scanning model according to which the MutS complex (made up of the hMSH2 and GTBP proteins, both of which are homologues of the bacterial MutS protein) binds to a mismatch and bidirectionally searches along the DNA for the signal that will direct incision to one of the two strands. The human MutS complex recognises, in addition to all 8 possible normal base mismatches, 112 base loops as well as pairs involving a damaged base such as $0 ^ { 6 }$ -methylguanine : T or C, $\mathrm { O ^ { 4 } }$ -methylthymine: A (but not $\mathbf { G }$ and 1,2-GpG adducts of cis-platin. However, it does not recognise 1,2-ApG, or 1,3-adducts of cis-platin or 1,3-adducts of trans-platin. These studies indicate the increasing interest in the possible involvement of mismatch repair in tumour resistance to alkylating drugs. Examples were given of cell lines in which drug sensitivity appeared to correlate with mismatch repair deficiency.

Progress in the production of cell lines and mice deficient in mismatch repair was described by te Riele (Amsterdam). $m s h \bar { 2 } ^ { - } / { ^ - }$ ES cells show the anticipated characteristics, including microsatellite instability, increased recombination frequency and methylation tolerance. Heterozygous, homozygous and chimeric msh2 knockout mice have been produced which do not show any overt abnormalities at birth. However, the homozygous animals have a predisposition to spontaneous carcinogenesis, developing mainly T-cell-derived lymphosarcomas as well as other types of tumours, including tumours of the lung, intestine and stomach. Unlike the human situation, heterozygous animals do not show an abnormal cancer susceptibility, while chimaeric animals have an intermediate phenotype. The interaction between loss of mismatch repair function and other cancer susceptibility traits in the natural history of carcinogenesis was indicated by the observation that crosses of the $m s h 2 ^ { - } \mathrm { ~ \AA ~ } ^ { - }$ mice with $m i n ^ { - }$ mice (heterozygous for the apc gene which is implicated in colon carcinogenesis) develop multiple intestinal tumours, demonstrating that msh2 deficiency accelerates intestinal carcinogenesis in a min\~ background.

Iaccarino et al. (Rome) reported the cDNA sequence for a $\mathbf { G } { : } \mathbb { T } ( \mathbb { U } )$ mismatch DNA glycosylase which also binds to $\mathrm { G } { : } 5$ -bromouracil and $\mathrm { O } ^ { 6 } .$ -methylguanine : T pairs. This cDNA is not related to any other known enzyme and may be involved in the repair of $\mathrm { G } \colon \mathrm { T }$ mismatches caused by deamination of 5-methylcytosine. Two mismatch repair activities have been identified in S. pombe by Fleck et al. (Berne), one of which can bind to and correct all types of mismatches (except $\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { C } )$ as well as DNA loops, while the other is specific for C-containing mismatches.

M. Bignami et al. (Rome) reported that methylation tolerant, mismatch repair-deficient human HeLa cells have increased rates of spontaneous somatic recombination. From the same laboratory Aquilina et al. (Rome, IARC, ICRF and Leiden) described the identification of two complementation groups among methylation tolerant cells. Complementation group I was hMLH1 deficient and had the anticipated characteristics (inability to repair $\mathrm { G } : \mathrm { T }$ mismatches or carry out repair synthesis at $O ^ { 6 }$ -methylguanine residues, increased instability at dinucleotide repeats). On the other hand, complementation group II had normal G:T mismatch repair and $0 ^ { 6 }$ -methylguanine-induced repair synthesis, but demonstrated lower tolerance to MNNG than group I cells and instability at mononucleotide (but not at dinucleotide) repeats. The authors proposed the hypothesis that $\mathbf { O } ^ { 6 } .$ -methylguanine : T and ${ \mathrm { O } } ^ { 6 } .$ -methylguanine : C pairs may be recognised by different complexes (involving hMSH2 in combination with GTBP for the first and a different protein for the second) and that group II cells are GTBP deficient and thus can tolerate the former but not the latter $\mathrm { O } ^ { 6 }$ -methylguanine pairs.

An observation of possible clinical significance was reported by Hampson et al. (ICRF and Oxford), who found that in cell lines established from human colorectal carcinomas, loss of $\beta 2$ -microglobulin (mediator of the recognition by thc immune system of non-self peptides) expression was highly correlated with mismatch repair defects and that microsatellite instability was over-represented among tumours deficient in $\beta 2$ -microglobulin. These observations imply the existence of strong immune response against tumours with genetic mismatch repair defects and suggest a way by which this response may be evaded by the tumours, namely by loss of $\beta 2$ -microglobulin.
6.2. Base excision repair (BER)

Lindahl (ICRF) reviewed the enzymology of base excision repair and described the in vitro reconstitution of this process (for the repair of a uracil-containing substrate) using purified human uracil-DNA glycosylase, AP endonuclease I, DNA polymerase $\beta$ , XRCC1 and DNA ligase III. The reaction was rapid and resulted in the replacement of a single nucleotide. It was suggested that the XRCCI protein can act as a scaffold holding polymerase $\beta$ and ligase III together and it was shown that it can stop chain displacement by polymerase $\beta$ The role of pol $\beta$ in BER was described by Wilson (Galveston). An $8 \ \mathrm { \ k D a }$ domain of pol $\beta$ contains dRPase activity, which is required to remove the $5 ^ { \prime } .$ -deoxyribose sugar left at the $5 ^ { \prime }$ terminus of the DNA following AP endonuclease activity. Mouse pol $\beta$ knockouts are embryonic lethal, but embryonic fibroblast lines have been established from them. They are sensitive to simple alkylating agents and unable to carry out BER, confirming the role of pol $\beta$ in this process. During fractionation of cell extracts, $10 \%$ of pol $\beta$ was found in a complex with DNA ligase I, raising the possibility of a role for ligase I as well as ligase III in BER.

Erixon et al. (Stockholm and Richmond) investigated the effects of polymerase inhibitors in mammalian cells treated with methylating agents. In repair proficient human or hamster cells and in XP cells aphidicolin (APC) and araC caused strand breaks, suggesting that a polymerase other than $\beta$ is involved in the repair of methylation products in DNA. However, dideoxythymidine also causes strand breaks indicating that polymerase $\beta$ is also involved. The amount of breaks resulting from AraC and 3-aminobenzamide, an inhibitor of poly(ADP-ribosyl) polymerase were additive, suggesting two parallel pathways in base excision repair.
6.2.1. Alkylpurine DNA glycosylases

The substrate specificity of alkylpurine DNA glycosylases was addressed by a number of laboratories. O'Connor et al. (Villejuif, Summit and Gyongsang, Korea) found that the E. coli 3-methyladenine glycosylase (AlkA), but not the human or rat methylpurine glycosylase, could removc damage induced by a number of clinically important nitrogen mustards and restore template activity for DNA replication. On the other hand. Cussac and F. Laval (Villejuif) reported that the Fpg protein, but not the AlkA protein, could protect bacteria from the toxic or mutagenic effects of the direct-acting alkylating agent aziridine, suggesting that aziridine induces fapy-type lesions in DNA. Finally, a poster from the J. Laval laboratory (Villejuif) indicated that, while the AlkA protein can excise hypoxanthine from DNA in vitro, it cannot protect $E .$ coli cells against nitrous acid-induced A to G mutations which are assumed to arise from deamination of adenine to hypoxanthine.

Strikingly, protection against this type of mutagenic effect was afforded by the uurA gene implying that. if the observed mutations are due to hypoxanthine, a DNA lesion chemically as minor as the deamination of adenine can be recognised and corrected by the UvrABC system.
Alkylpurine-DNA-glycosylase knockout mice have been generated by Elder et al. (Manchester). They are viable and fertile. Their phenotype is under investigation.
6.2.2. Uracil-DNA glycosylase

Recent information on the structure of human uracil-DNA glycosylase revealed a highly conserved DNA-binding groove and an essentially invariant uracil-binding pocket. Krokan et al. (Trondheim and La Jolla) presented biochemical data indicating active flipping of U out of the DNA helix and into the recognition pocket. Furthermore, the substrate specificity of the enzyme could be changed by single amino acid substitutions to give rise to mutants that recognised either C or $\mathrm { T }$ in DNA substrate. When these mutants were expressed in $E .$ coli they were cytotoxic and mutagenic. The sequence specificity of $E$ coli uracil-DNA glycosylase was examined by Nilsen et al. from the same laboratory (1C.8), and the consensus for good and bad repair found to be ${ \mathsf { S } } ^ { \prime } ( { \mathrm { A } } / { \mathrm { T } } ) { \mathrm { U A } } ( { \mathrm { A } } / { \mathrm { T } } ) 3 ^ { \prime }$ and ${ \sf 5 ^ { \prime } ( G / C ) } \mathrm { U ( T / G / C ) } 3 ^ { \prime }$ , respectively. The sequence specificity of repair correlated well with the sequence distribution of U-induced mutations along the lacl gene.
6.2.3. Oxidative DNA damage

Luna et al. (Oslo) reported the isolation of human cDNA's with homology to the bacterial DNA glycosylase genes fpg and nth. Sequence analyses indicate that the DNA-binding motifs present in the bacterial Fpg and Nth, a zinc finger and the 4Fe-4S cluster, respectively, are conserved in the corresponding human enzymes. The same group (Eide et al.) also reported the isolation from S. cerevisiae of a gene (SCNTH) for a DNA glycosylase from yeast which is similar to endonuclease III from E. coli. The expressed protein of $4 5 \ \mathrm { k D a }$ removed thymine glycols as well as ring-opened 7-methylguanine (fapy) residues like the $E .$ coli Fpg enzyme, but, in contrast to the latter, did not remove 8-oxoguanine. Boiteux et al. (Villejuif and Gif) reported on a S.

cerevisiae gene, OGGl, a functional homologue of the bacterial fpg gene. OGGl encodes a DNA glycosylase/AP lyase that excises 8-oxoguanine and fapy. This $4 3 \ \mathrm { \ k D a }$ enzyme preferentially excises 8-oxoguanine opposite cytosine or thymine but not opposite adenine. A mutant of this gene has a hypermutable phenotype and causes $\mathbf { G } : \mathbf { C }$ to $\mathbf { T } : \mathbf { A }$ transversions.
6.2.4. Human $A P$ -endonuclease I (HAP1)

HAP1, cloned by Hickson and coworkers (ICRF. Oxford), is the major human AP-endonuclease and it is a homologue of exonuclease III in $E .$ coli. The enzyme also has $3 ^ { \prime }$ phosphodiesterase, $3 ^ { \prime }$ -phosphatase and Rnase H activity. In addition, HAPI possesses the ability to alter the redox state of a conserved cysteine residue located in the DNA-binding domain of c-Jun and c-Fos. Repair and redox domains are structurally and functionally distinct. Based on homology with exonuclease III, a model for the structure of HAP1 has been established and critical amino acid residues in the proposed active site identified by site-directed mutagenesis.
6.2.5. DNA ligases

By knocking out DNA ligase I in mice, Melton et al. (Edinburgh) showed that haematopoiesis was disrupted and this led to prenatal death after mid-term. Thus, DNA ligase I is required for normal mammalian development, but is not entirely essential for DNA replication, indicating that, in case of its absence. other ligases may complement this defect during DNA replication. The cloning of two human DNA ligase genes (including a previously unknown one) was discussed by Lindahl and coworkers. Using information from peptide sequences from a region that is conserved in all known eukaryotic DNA ligases, two human cDNA's were isolated and ex pressed, one of which encoded the previously described DNA ligase III of $1 0 3 \mathrm { \ k D a }$ that interacts with XRCC1. The other cDNA encoded a new ATP-dependent ligase of $9 6 ~ \mathrm { \ k D a }$ DNA ligase IV. DNA ligases III and IV share a related active site motif and several short regions of homology with DNA ligase I. DNA ligases III and IV are located on human chromosomes $1 7 \mathrm { q } 1 1 . 2 \mathrm { - } 1 2$ and 13q33-34. respectively.
6.2.6. Expression of alkyltransferases

Several groups reported progress in the biology of alkylation damage repair in eukaryotes. Rafferty et al. (Manchester) described the induction by X-rays of $0 ^ { 6 }$ -methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) in various tissues of p53-deficient mice. They found that, while the basal levels of the enzyme did not depend on the animals' p53 status, induction was absolutely dependent on p53 expression, implying that p53 may modulate the expression of MGMT. Grombacher et al. (Mainz and Galveston) reported on the induction of MGMT in rat hepatoma cells H4IIE by MNNG, X-rays and dexamethasone and a lack of co-regulation with $N .$ methylpurineDNA glycosylase. The presence of two alternative transcripts of $N .$ -methylpurine-DNA glycosylase in human cell lines was described by Pelkonen et al. (IARC. Lyon). The proportions of the two types of transcripts varied between different cell lines and did not correlate with overall enzymatic activity.
6.2.7. Practical applications of DNA repair studies

It is reasonable to anticipate that individual ability to repair DNA lesions may play a critical role in the determination of clinical response to antitumour alkylating agents. Buschfort et al. (Essen) presented data relevant to this question using lymphocytes of CLL patients. A battery of in vitro assays for DNA repair activity (adduct repair at single-cell level. induction and loss of repair-related single-strand breaks by the comet assay, DNA incision in a damaged plasmid) were employed. and good correlation with the in vitro sensitivity to alkylating agent as well as indications of a correlation with clinical response to alkylating drug treatment were obtained.

Collins et al. (Aberdeen) described how the comet assay can be exploited to study DNA lesions other than strand breaks in the context of molecular epidemiology as well as more fundamental investigations by treating nucleoids with enzymes capable of converting specific lesions (e.g.. E. coli fpg for 8-oxoguanine. T4 endonuclease V for cyclobutane dimers) into single-strand breaks that can be subsequently quantitated with high sensitivity. Using these modifications of the comet assay to measure different lesions, Dusinska et al. (Bratislava. Teplice and Aberdeen) examined DNA repair capacity in groups of patients with different chronic degenerative diseases which are possibly related to oxidative stress. In peripheral lymphocytes derived from diabetes and ankylosing spondylitis patients, the endogenous levels of these DNA lesions were higher than in healthy individuals. In addition, no repair of strand breaks was found in ankylosing spondelytis patients. These preliminary results indicate that the comet assay provides a practical method for assessing endogenous DNA damage and repair capacities in human cells.
7. Repair of strand breaks
7.1. DNA-PK

Jeggo et al. (MRC Brighton) discussed the role of the multi-component DNA-dependent kinase (DNAPK) in cellular responses. Mutants defective in two of the components $\mathrm { K u } 8 6$ and $\mathrm { D N A - P K } _ { \mathrm { c s } }$ , encoded by the genes XRCC5 and XRCC7, respectively) are very sensitive to ionising radiation and have defects in V(D)J recombination. A mammalian mutant for the third component $\left( \mathrm { K u } 7 0 \right)$ has yet to be identified. XRCC7 has a $1 4 ~ \mathrm { \mathbf { k } \mathbf { b } }$ ORF with a kinase domain at the carboxy-terminus and belongs to the PI3 kinaselike family. $\mathbf { K } \mathbf { u } 7 0$ and 86 form a complex with affinity for ds DNA ends or other discontinuities, suggesting that these components recognize strand interruptions leading to activation of the kinase component. The in vivo substrates of the kinase activity remain a matter of speculation.

Errami et al. (Leiden) showed that independently-isolated Chinese hamster V79 mutants belonging to complementation group 5 have mutations in the $\mathtt { K u 8 6 }$ gene. The different alleles show different levels of X-ray sensitivity. Two of these mutants produce mRNA with in-frame deletions corresponding to the loss of 46 and 84 amino acids, respectively. Blunt et al. (MRC, Brighton) have identified mouse and hamster homologues of XRCC7. which predict $83 \%$ identity in the $3 ^ { \prime }$ kinase domain to the human protein. Mutants defective in XRCC7, such as the scid (severe combined immune deficient) mouse and the hamster V3 line have different mutations, since scid expresses DNA-PK at near wild-type levels while V3 has much reduced levels. A nonsense mutation potcntially responsible for the scid phenotype has been identified in the highly conserved carboxy-terminal domain of DNA-PKcs.

A mutant of S. cerevisiae, known as hdfl, has sequence similarity to $\mathbf { K } \mathbf { u } 7 0$ Friedl et al. (Oberschleissheim) showed that haploid hdfl and diploid hdfl rad52 knockout mutants are very radiation-sensitive while diploid hdfl mutants are not. The hdfl rad52 mutants degrade irradiated DNA and show low frequencies of chromosomal aberrations, but the rad52 mutant has no degradation and a high frequency of aberrations, suggesting that Hdf1 protects broken ends but promotes aberration formation. Thus, although the major pathway for DSB repair in S. cerevisiae involves homologous recombination, a homology-independent DNA end joining mechanism can also contribute to DSB repair.
7.2. Genes involved in DNA cross-link repair in humans

Thompson et al. (Livermore) have isolated cDNAs that partially correct mutants with sensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents; these cDNAs are candidates for the genes known as XRCC2, XRCC3, and XRCC9. The cDNAs relating to XRCC2 and XRCC3 have limited homology to the S. cerevisiae recombination gene RAD5l and its human homologue HsRAD51, and encode proteins of 280 and 346 amino acids, respectively. The cDNA relating to XRCC9 has no known homology.

Thacker et al. (MRC Harwell) have also isolated cDNAs relating to the XRCC2 gene, using a positional cloning approach. Having first finely mapped the gene to chromosome $7 9 3 6 . 1$ , they have localized it to a single YAC giving complete correction of the mutant defect. A large number of cDNAs isolated by direct selection with the YAC were sequenced to identify candidates for the gene.

Arwert et al. (Amsterdam) examined the genetic basis of the reversion of MMC sensitivity in Fanconi anemia, group C patients with apparent mosaicism, by comparing mutations in the $F A C$ gene in MMCsensitive and MMC-resistant cells. The results indicated that two distinct types of genetic recombination: intragenic mitotic recombination and gene conversion were responsible for the presence of a wildtype allele of the $F A C$ gene in MMC-resistant cells.
7.3. PARP and XRCC1

De Murcia (Strasbourg) discussed the function of the enigmatic protein poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is rapidly synthesised in response to DNA strand breaks. PARP catalyses the transfer of ADP-ribose from the respiratory coenzyme $\mathrm { \ N A D ^ { + } }$ to certain DNA-binding proteins and to itself. The protein has two zinc fingers at the N-terminus to act as a nick-sensor and a C-terminal catalytic domain whose activity is strongly stimulated on binding to DNA breaks. The crystal structure of chicken PARP has been solved to show that it is related to bacterial ADP-ribosylating toxins. Data from dominant-negative mutants, knockout mice, and the search for protein interactions suggest that PARP coordinates cellular responses to DNA damage with cell-cycle progression.

Dantzer et al. (Strasbourg) prescnted evidencc for the role of PARP in DNA replication, through its interaction with the p180 subunit of DNA polymerase $\alpha \mathrm { . }$ -primase complex, suggesting a role in the detection of damage with the progression of the replication fork.

The phenotype of mutants defective in XRCC1 protein is consistent with its role in a late stage of base-excision repair, and the protein has been shown to physically interact with DNA ligase III. Ligase III has a zinc-finger motif recognizing strand breaks in vitro, with homology to the nick-sensing motifs on PARP. Caldecott and Nash (Manchester and ICRF South Mimms) have found that PARP appears to associate with the XRCC1/ligase III complex and that PARP activity is inhibited by ligase III. They suggest that these three proteins act as a nick-sensing mechanism in damaged cells.

Thompson et al. (Livermore) have generated XRCC1 knockouts. Null embryos died by E9.5 having failed to gastrulate normally at E6.5. This very severe phenotype was unexpected, especially given that DNA ligase I knockouts develop normally to E12.5, and implies that XRCC1 is involved in processes additional to DNA repair. The phenotype of DNA ligase III knockouts will be particularly informative. There was preliminary evidence for increased rates of apoptosis in the XRCCl null embryos.

It has been found recently that PARP is an early marker of apoptosis, through cleavage by proteases of the Ced3/ICE family. Scovassi's group (Pavia) has characterized the apoptotic events occurring in human tumour cell lines after different lethal stimuli (antitumour drugs, serum starvation, growth arrest). Following the characteristic appearance of high molecular weight DNA fragments, PARP is activated. The enhancement of the automodification capacity of the PARP is followed by proteolytic cleavage of the enzyme. This indicates that the apoptotic cell programme is associated with modulation of post-translational modifications.

Shah et al. (Sainte-Foy. Quebec) have developed an activity-based method for detection of the apoptotic $( 8 9 ~ \mathrm { k D a } )$ fragment of PARP, and have shown that this fragment does not act as a nick sensor. Paris et al. (Gif-sur-Yvette) used this assay to investigate the radiation sensitivity of cell lines differing in p53 status, and showcd that apoptosis was more rapid in cells with enhanced radiosensitivity.

The involvement of PARP in familial Adenomatous Polyposis was examined by Cristovao et al. (Lisbon) by analyzing the effect of gamma rays on $\mathbf { N A D } ^ { + }$ levels of peripheral leukocytes. No stimulation of PARP by gamma-irradiation was found in FAP patients. The significant increase in the level of $\mathrm { N A D ^ { + } }$ and total NAD after 3AB (an inhibitor of PARP) treatment was found only in healthy individuals, and no such response was seen in FAP patients. The results imply a difference in redox potential of FAP cells or a defect for $\mathrm { N A D } ^ { + }$ consumption due to PARP synthesis in these patients.
7.4. Cloning and analysis of genes related to yeast recombination repair genes

Kooistra et al. (Leiden) have cloned a homologue of RAD54 from $D$ melanogaster. using degenerate PCR primers from yeast conserved sequences. Identity with the human and mouse proteins is about $5 0 \%$ overall, with greater homology in the helicase domains. The gene is located at chromosome II23D, close to the Rrp1 AP-endonuclease gene. Expression of the gene was highest in early embryos and females, suggesting that the gene has a role in meiotic recombination and/or in fertilization-associated replication.

Essers et al. (Rotterdam) showed that the human homologue of the S. cerevisiae RAD54 gene predicts a protein with $48 \%$ identity to the yeast protein, and similarly belongs to the SNF2 family of DNA-dependent ATPases. Vispe et al. (Toulouse) have cloned the Chinese hamster Rad5l gene, showing that this is similar to mouse and human homologues. Treatment of cells with DNA damaging agents such as $N$ -methyl $. N ^ { \prime }$ -nitro $N -$ -nitrosoguanidine and MMC appears to lead to an induction of the gene product.

The S. pombe homologues of S. cerevisiae RAD51, RAD52 and RAD54 have been studied by Vreeken et al. (Leiden, Brighton and Braunschweig). Knockout mutants of the RAD51 and RAD54 homologues (rhp51 and rhp54, respectively) have similar phenotypes in the two yeasts, but a knockout mutant of the RAD52 homologue (rad22) is less severe. Although not essential for viability, a mini-chromosome loss assay showed that the rhp51 and rhp54 mutants have a very high level of spontaneous chromosome loss. The response of double mutants of rhp54 with checkpoint genes chkl or rad17 suggested that Rhp54 is likely to be involved in DNA replication.

By evolutionary walking, McKay et al. (Rotterdam) have cloned homologues of the S. pombe rad2l gene, involved in repair of radiation-induced DNA breaks. Predicted human and S. pombe genes showed $2 5 \%$ identity overall, but with the N-terminal region (where the original yeast mutation occurred) showing $59 \%$ homology. The human gene is cellcycle regulated but is not inducible by radiation. The mouse gene is expressed in all tissues (3.1 kb transcript), and especially testis and thymus, suggesting a role in recombination, but a smaller transcript is expressed at a high lcvcl in post-meiotic spermatids. This gene is located on human chromosome 8q24 and mouse 15D3.

Clever et al. (Bern) showed that over-expression of wild-type or mutant Rad54 protein in wild-type S. cerevisiae cells is detrimental, possibly implicating Rad54 in protein—protein interactions. Using a 2-hybrid screen, potential candidates for this interaction were identified; one of which had $\beta$ -transducin repeats. Disruption of the ORFs encoding the candidate proteins resulted in an MMS sensitive phenotype.
The S. cerevisiae RAD51 gene is induced following ionising or UV radiation, but induction of a
RAD5l fusion gene was markedly reduced in rad52 mutant cells suggesting that DNA damage processing precedes induction (Averbeck and Averbeck, Paris).

Ahne (Oberschleissheim) showed that the rad54-1 mutant of S. cerevisiae was very inefficient at the correct repair of DNA double-strand gaps in marker plasmids. Similarly rev2 (rad5) mutants gave only about $20 \%$ correct repair of this substrate. Sequence analysis of the incorrectly repaired products revealed that in most cases the break ends were blunted before joining, but sometimes there were deletions or insertions at the break site. The fidelity function of REV2 may be important in determining the sensitivity of these mutants.

Nairn (Smithville) made CHO cell lines that are defective in ERCCl. These lines show the expected sensitivity to UV and MMC. The results of gene targeting experiments at the APRT locus implied a role for ERCC1 in recombination, analogous to that of Rad10 in S. cerevisiae.

Willson et al. (Brighton) reported the isolation of 121 MMS sensitive S. pombe mutants. Many of the mutants are cross-sensitive to UV and gamma-rays: G2 checkpoint and recombination classes of mutants are represented in the collection. A plasmid was isolated that complemented one of the mutants (mms64) that is unable to arrest in G2 after treatment with ionising radiation.
7.5. Mammalian Holliday junction resolvase

Davies et al. (ICRF, South Mimms) purified a 38 kDa protein related to the $E .$ coli RuvC protein from rodent cell lines and calf testes. A number of other proteins were also found to bind labelled Holliday junctions, but it is not clear if these specifically recognize junctions or other features such as bent DNA. Resolvase activity was found at normal levels in a series of ionising radiation-sensitive cell lines and human mutant lines.
7.6. DNA double-strand break rejoining by mammalian cell extracts

Johnson and Fairman (MRC, Harwell) proposed that double-strand break repair is mediated by complexes including ligases and accessory proteins. They have identified two types of activity involved in the repair of simple double-strand breaks: activities that directly join breaks and an activity (REP-1) that stimulates joining. The rejoining activities surprisingly do not show the characteristic adenylation products of DNA ligases, and the stimulation given to a pure ligase by REP-1 is correlated with the loss of adenylation product.

Mason et al. (MRC, Harwell) have studied the rejoining of double-strand breaks with non-complementary ends. The efficiency of rejoining of such breaks was dependent on the type of break end $( 5 ^ { \prime }$ overhang, $3 ^ { \prime }$ overhang or blunt); some ends were rejoined through blunting of single-stranded ends followed by ligation, while others rejoined through illegitimate recombination between short direct repeat sequences. Proteins involved in the repeat-driven mechanism were partially purified by fractionation of calf thymus extracts.
7.7. Techniques and applications

Using graded-field gel electrophoresis DahmDaphi and Dikomey (Hamburg) showed that the efficiency of the repair of DSBs introduced by X-rays in DNA of CHO cells does not depend on the length of the DNA fragments.

Arrand et al. (Brunel and Northwood) have looked at microsatellite length polymorphisms in a number of human genes implicated in repair of ionising radiation induced DNA damage. Among patients who showed a severe adverse reaction to radiotherapy they have identified 2 patients heterozygous for rare repeat-length polymorphisms in the XRCC1 and XRCC5 genes. Microsatellite repeat-length polymorphisms could possibly provide a tool for the development of a predictive assay for radiosensitivity.
8. Perturbation of cellular processes by DNA damage
8.1. Checkpoints
In addition to disturbing the primary structure of DNA, damaging agents induce a complex, prolonged and variable response in pro- and eukaryote cells.

The resulting concerted action of protective mechanisms provides the cell with ways to survive damage (repair, tolerance, cycle delay), or to die via a regulated apoptosis. The acceptable level of residual DNA damage consistent with survival may require the induction of mechanisms which, while permitting DNA metabolism to proceed, introduce mutations and reduce genetic integrity. The precise balance of these concerted actions and their outcomes may differ radically from one cell type to another and among different organisms. Because of their importance (to the survival of the organism) we might expect the integration of the concerted actions as well as the particular actions themselves to be the subjects of intense natural selection.

It is, therefore, not surprising to learn that checkpoint genes in both fission and budding yeast may also be involved in DNA metabolism or repair functions. Experiments reported by Lydall (Tucson) on cdc13 mutants of S. cerevisiae, which spontaneously generate telomeric DNA damage, show that the RAD9-dependent G2 checkpoint is induced by action of the Rad17 exonuclease (another checkpoint protein) on this substrate. rad9 mutations suppress the activity of Radl7, the checkpoint-inducing signal is not produced and cells progress to mitosis where they die of accumulated DNA damage. Interestingly. the existence in S. cerevisiae of a RAD9 controlled network analogous to the $E .$ coli SOS system has been reported by Lowndes (ICRF, South Mimms, and Paris). Indeed, RAD9 is required not only for the activation of the G1, S and G2 checkpoints in the cell cycle but also for the transcriptional response to DNA damage. Dun1, a transducer of DNA damage transcriptional response of RNR1, RNR2 and RNR3 genes is part of this RAD9 control. It is important to note that even after functional substitution of checkpoints, the rad9 mutant remains UV-sensitive indicating that a further role of $R A D 9$ (such as transcriptional activation) plays a major role in the response to UV.

Further progress in understanding the nature of the DNA structure checkpoints was discussed by Carr (MRC, Brighton). In fission yeast the checkpoint depends on six genes (radl, rad3, rad9, rad7, rad26 and hus1) which collectively sense DNA alterations or replication arrest. Several of the checkpoint genes bear structural homologies either to replication proteins (Rad17 with RFC). to PI 3-kinase like proteins (Rad3), or to protein kinases (Chk1 /Rad27). The similarity of the rad3 mutant phenotype to that of the human disease, ataxiatelangiectasia (A-T), and the homology between the Rad3 and ATM gene products. emphasizes the central role of PI3-kinase like proteins in establishing the damage response of eukaryotic cells. Clearly checkpoints can be subverted by changing the phosphorylation status of key checkpoint sensing proteins, which is the reason for the intense interest in the development and analysis of specific protein kinase inhibitors discussed by Abbondandolo (Genoa).

Defective S-phase responses of A-T cells to DNA damage were reported by Dixon (Cincinnati) and Paterson (Edmonton). The Dixon group first described the UV-induced hyperphosphorylation of the p34 subunit of the RPA replication protein. a credible substrate for the DNA-PK enzyme. and reported that in A-T cells, which fail to arrest DNA synthesis after damage. RPA is not hyperphosphorylated. These findings suggest that both the ATM gene product and DNA-PK operate in the signalling pathway that identifies DNA damage or structural abnormalities in S-phase nuclei. Work by the Paterson group emphasized the importance of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II pathway in signalling thc radiation-induced delay in the S-phase of normal cells, and also that this pathway is defective in A-T cells. Interestingly, while the relative positions of the calmodulin kinase Il and ATM elements of the signalling pathway are uncertain, only the S-phase checkpoint requires the participation of calmodulin kinase II.

Cloning the gene defective in A-T. a tour de force, was described by Shiloh (Tel Aviv). The structure of the ATM gene is one of considerable complexity; it has two promoters, one bidirectional, as well as two active internal promoters. ATM transcripts show multiple alternative ${ \mathsf { J } } ^ { \prime } { \mathsf { U T R s } }$ and alternative polyadenylation signals which give rise to $3 ^ { \prime }$ UTRs of variable lengths. The possibility of many different $5 ^ { \prime }$ -transcripts of the ATM gene suggests that a rapid, subtle and sensitive translational regulation of the proteins may be possible in response to a variety of cell stress conditions. resulting in the precise modulation of ATM catalytic activity in association with different substrates. The search is now on for ATM-interacting proteins, and there is a strong suspicion that mild ATM mutations may be responsible for other (? cancer-prone) phenotypes distinct from A-T.
8.2. DNA damage and replication

The S-phase checkpoint ensures that DNA synthesis rapidly terminates and is not completed for many hours. Experiments reported by Orren ct al. (Baltimore) on UV6I and UV5 Chinese hamster cell mutants and also wild-type cells showed that following UV-irradiation of S-phase cells. DNA synthesis is eventually completed, presumably by a translesion mechanism, but that (6-4) photoproducts presented a greater problem for replication than CPDs. For human cells. Squires et al. (Cambridge) reported that CPDs induced in active replicons caused rapid stalling of ongoing replication forks. Stalling was overcome over a period of several hours in repaircompetent cells. but in XP-A cells most of the stalled forks were converted to frank double-strand breaks. The kinetics of recovery from stalling were found to be related to the operation of a replication-coupled repair pathway operating two- to threefold faster than global repair. This pathway is defective in CS and is normal in XP-C cells. These data suggest that. as with RNA polymerase II stalling at CPDs. the arrest of DNA polymerases at these lesions signals the rapid recruitment of the NER machinery.

In contrast to the promotion of error-free replication by facilitated repair. there was new genetic and biochemical evidence for the operation of error-prone translesion mechanisms in bacteria and S. cereriside. Livneh (Rehovot) reported the in vitro reconstruction of an error-prone NER mechanism in $E$ coli. operating on templates damaged on both strands. The key mutagenic component in this translesion synthesis reaction is DNA polymerase III core enzyme. Lawrence (Rochester) has discovered a new mutagenic DNA polymerase in yeast. DNA polymerase $\zeta$ , presumably operating via a translesion mechanism. Polymerase $\zeta$ turns out to be a complex formed by the Rev3 and Rev7 gene products. The new enzyme has DNA polymerase activity in vitro. and is able to replicate past a thymine-thymine cis-syn cyclobutane dimer (a lesion that normally severely inhibits replication), with an efficiency of around $1 0 \%$ . far greater than other polymerases. The likelihood that translesion synthesis has a genetic basis in all eukaryotes is strengthened by the finding of $R E V . ^ { 3 } / R E V 7$ homologues in man, while Pastink (Leiden) reported the identification of a Drosophila gene ( mus205) which bears considerable homology to REV3.
8.3. Damage-inducible genes

A number of groups provided new insights into the nature of proteins induced by DNA damage. Kaina's group (Mainz) investigated whether the damage inducible proto-oncogene c-fos is involved in protecting cells from the genotoxic effects of UV radiation. Mouse fibroblasts deficient in $c ^ { * }$ -fos were hypersensitive to UV-induced lethality. clastogenicity, and recovery from the arrest of DNA replication. In contrast. c-fos deficient cells are as efficient as the wild-type in DNA repair synthesis for doses below $3 0 ~ \mathrm { J m } ~ \overset { \cdot } { ^ { 3 } }$ . They suggested that the hypersensitive phenotype of $\dot { \ell }$ -Fos-deficient cells is primarily a consequence of impaired S-phase checkpoint control after UV treatment.

The ability of three alkylpurines to inhibit the activity of specific protein kinases was examined by Abbondandolo's group (Genoa). The compounds chosen do not damage DNA but affect early and late events of the cell cycle in rodent cells. The results indicate that S6 ribosomal protein phosphorylation by the $7 0  { ~ \mathrm { k D a } ~ }  { \mathrm { S 6 } }$ kinase and MAP kinase phosphorylation which plays a role in DNA synthesis and mitosis are steps of independent pathways. Moreover. the major components of the cytoskeleton (actin. $\beta$ -tubulin and vimentin) were all affected by 6-dimethylamino purine while only the $\beta$ tubulin was altered by the $\mathrm { O ^ { 6 } }$ -methyl and ${ { \mathrm { O } } ^ { 6 } } .$ ethyl guanine. It is clear that non-DNA targets are involved in the effects of these compounds on early cell-cycle events and induction of chromosome loss.

The same group is involved in another project aiming at the isolation of CHO cells expressing DNA damage inducible genes (Menichini et al.). A gene-trapping strategy based on the use of a promoterless lacZ gene in transfection experiments has been applied to cells treated with UV and $\gamma$ rays. Clones expressing at least tenfold induction of $\beta$ . galactosidase were sorted by FACS-FDG analysis. One promising clone indicating a possible role of a growth factor or its receptor in the UV-response, has been selected and characterised.

The loss of p53-dependent suppressor function appears to be a frequent and critical step in the progression of many types of tumours. Several groups reported on the theme of how p53 dysfunction can affect genomic instability. The studies of Verhaegh and Hainaut (Lyon) stressed the remarkable conformational flexibility of p53. Human breast tumour cells, expressing wild-type p53 accumulated p53 in a form immunologically identical to 'mutant' p53 upon treatment with the zinc chelating agent TPEN. Further studies showed that p53 could also be modulated by redox conditions. Clearly changes in such environmental conditions could contribute to apparent dysfunction of p53, although the cellular consequences of 'mutant-like' changes in p53 protein conformation, such as loss of checkpoint integrity, have yet to be proven.

Preservation of genome integrity relies upon the efficient coordination of damage signalling and repair pathways during replication on damaged templates. Johnson et al. (Cambridge, Cardiff and Smithville) have highlighted a potential role for p53 in controlling the course of events following the stalling of replication forks at CPDs. Not only does loss of wild-type p53 function correlate with significant reduction of excision repair ability of CPDs and (6-4) photoproducts but tumour or SV40 transformed cells can generate frank double-strand breaks at stalled forks. The presence of wild-type p53 reduces the extent of break generation in stalled forks, providing a possible role for maintaining genome stability.

Chin and Smith (Cardiff) presented studies on the comparative cell-cycle effects of DNA damaging and non-damaging inhibitors of DNA topoisomerase II. p53 was not required for the arrest of cells at a catenation-sensitive G2 checkpoint although the presence of wild-type p53, stabilized in response to topoisomerase inhibition rather than DNA damage, permitted the efficient expression of apoptosis. The studies also revealed the triggering of apoptosis in early S-phase as a consequence of topoisomerase dysfunction, suggesting a role for this enzyme in allowing normal replicon dynamics.

Although p53 has a central role in both promoting apoptosis and cell-cycle checkpoint arrest, the studies of Rosselli et al. (Paris) suggested that the radiosensitivity of A-T cells, accompanied by a reduced or delayed p53 response, is not related to increased apoptosis. Furthermore, Fanconi anemia (FA) cells show an impairment of p53 stabilization after exposure to MMC, a chemical agent for which FA cells demonstrate a specific cellular and chromosomal hypersensitivity. It appears that sensitivity to genotoxic agents and drugs which disrupt dynamic changes in chromatin conformation, can be affected both by p53 function and dysfunction. The session highlighted the need to understand the integrating role of important molecules such as p53 in permitting the processes of cycle arrest and cell death to be interfaced with lesion and stress-handling pathways.
9 Mutagenesis

Whilst most contributors confined their attention to a particular repair system, Devoret et al. (Gif) proposed a global model for bacteria integrating NER, homologous recombination repair and mutagenic SOS repair. These are proposed to operate as a cascade in time after exposure to an agent such as UV. An important feature of this model is that stoichiometric considerations suggested that the $\mathrm { U m u D } _ { \geq } ^ { \prime } \mathbf { C }$ complex is envisaged as binding to a lesion at the end of the filament of RecA protein which has formed around a post-replication gap. This then acts as an inhibitor of recombination and switches repair into the mutagenic SOS mode.

Devoret's model had no room for mutations arising at a low level during NER although Retel et al. (Amsterdam) addressed this. This question remains controversial although Retel et al. argued that it was implicit in their observation that $\mathbf { G } : \mathbf { C }$ to $\mathbf { C } : \mathbf { G }$ transversions were found when plasmids containing lacZ (or lacl) genes were exposed to gamma radiation either intracellularly or after transfection in NER-proficient but not in NER-deficient bacteria.
9.1. Mutation spectra

Differences in mutational spectra were observed between NER-proficient and NER-deficient cells with a variety of different systems, e.g., bacteria treated with chloroethyl-cyclohexyl-nitroso-urea (Iannone et al., Genoa and Cordoba), XP-D, TTD and wild-type human cells with UV-treated shuttle vectors (Stary et al., Villejuif), or with shuttle vectors containing 8- oxoguanine (Le Page et al., Villejuif IIIC13), UVBand UVA-treated ERCC1-deficient CHO cells (Sage et al., Paris and Montreal), p53 mutations in skin tumours from XP and normal subjects (DayaGrosjean et al., Villejuif). Interestingly, in all these systems, DNA repair deficiencies (XP cells or skin tumours, or CHO cells) were associated with a high level of CC to TT tandem mutations considered as a specific signature of UV-damage.

Interestingly the spectrum of mutations in an UV-irradiated shuttle vector transfected into TTD cells was closer to that seen following transfection into normal than into XP cells (Stary et al.). The unexplained difference between XP and TTD cells in susceptibility to sunlight-induced skin cancer is of fundamental interest and is usually interpreted in terms of the different nature of the genetic deficiencies causing differences in transcription, in turn possibly affecting immune surveillance (see Section 4). These results, however, suggest that there may be subtle differences between XP. and TTD cells in repair at different lesions or sites. Indeed, the 8-oxoguanine containing plasmid exhibited a higher mutation frequency in the TTD cell line as compared to normal or XP-C cells (Le Page et al.). Whether these differences are of relevance to skin cancer remains to be determined.

Pascucci and Dogliotti (Rome) have applied the difficult technique of RFLP/PCR mutation assay to human mitochondrial DNA. The spontaneous mutation frequency was $1 0 ^ { - 5 } – 1 0 ^ { - 6 }$ .Whereas spontaneous mutations were highly specific for certain bases, UV-induced mutations were mostly $\mathbf { C }$ to $\mathbf { T }$ as expected and were tenfold above the spontaneous level.

The availability of transgenic mouse models with integrated bacterial target genes has enabled experiments to be carried out that attempt to relate DNA lesions to carcinogenesis in the whole animal. Mientjes et al. (Zeist and Leiden) used lacZ mice and followed alkylated DNA and mutations in various organs after treatment with EMS, ENU and $N , N .$ -diethylnitrosamine. The results were complex and varied from organ to organ. For example, $\mathbf { O } ^ { 6 }$ ethylations were removed in liver and bone marrow by 3 days, but whereas in bone marrow the mutation frequency peaked at 3 days, in liver it continued to increase up to 28 days. Explanations based on different alkylation products make some sense, for example in bone marrow $41 \%$ of mutations were $\mathbf { G } : \mathbf { C }$ to $\mathsf { A } : \mathsf { T }$ transitions, possibly attributable to $0 ^ { 6 }$ guanine alkylations; in liver only $19 \%$ were $\mathbf { G } : \mathbb { C }$ to $\mathbf { A } : \mathbf { T }$ and the influence of $0 ^ { 2 }$ -thymine alkylations was postulated.

'Adaptive mutations' in bacteria are still an unknown process found in non-growing bacteria. Bridges (MRC, Brighton) showed that spontaneous mutations in non-growing bacteria were highly elevated in mutY /mutM double mutants (more than 100 times as compared to wild-type cells). The hypothesis, partly correlated with the types of mutations, is that 8-oxo-guanine was produced as a spontaneous lesion giving rise to mutated messenger RNA and to modified enzymes allowing DNA replication to start and to fix the 'adaptive' mutations. The same DNA lesion (8-oxoguanine) has been studied in Blanco's laboratory (Valencia) in oxyR bacteria. These bacteria are sensitive to oxidative stress which gives rise to two types of mutations. One class is SOS-dependent and is believed to be generated from abasic sites (mostly T : A to $\mathbf { A } : \mathbf { T }$ and $\mathbf { G } : \mathbf { C }$ to $\mathbf { A } : \mathrm { T } )$ and the other is SOS-independent but mutM / mutYdependent (G: C to $\mathrm { T } \colon \mathrm { A } )$ , and believed to be induced by unrepaired 8-oxoguanine.
9.2. Mechanisms of formation of chromosome aberrations

A novel system for testing mutagenicity in plants was described by Angelis et al. (Prague). Cotyledons of germinating tobacco seeds express somatic mutation by displaying coloured spots, allowing the quantification of a mutagenic response to MNU and MMS, as well as to MNNG which previously has been reported to be non-mutagenic in plants. Genetic modification of DNA repair pathways was envisaged as a means to further increase the sensitivity of the system.

Howard et al. (Cambridge and Berlin) reported that SV40 transformation of Indian muntjac cells results in chronic genomic instability and hypersensitivity to UV and DMS. Using alternating-field gel electrophoresis, it was demonstrated that DNA double-strand breaks appeared at the replication fork $1 2 { - } 1 6 \ \mathrm { h }$ after UV-irradiation in these cells, suggesting that they may be unable to accomplish competent replication of damaged DNA. In contrast, primary or spontaneously transformed cells did not show genomic instability, UV-hypersensitivity or late appearance of DNA double-strand breaks.

In a study of the mutagenic and genotoxic effects of theophylline in Chinese hamster V79 cells, Slamenova et al. (Bratislava) reported a dose-dependent increase of chromosome aberrations and DNA single-strand breaks, but no increase of HPRT gene mutation. Cells cultured in low concentration $( < 0 . 3$ $\mathrm { m g / m l } )$ of theophylline showed reduced rate of DNA replication and delayed rejoining of MNNGinduced DNA strand breaks, suggesting an inhibitory effect of theophylline on DNA replication and repair. The report of Darroudi et al. (Leiden) focused on the mechanisms by which ionizing radiation induces chromosome aberrations in human peripheral blood lymphocytes. Although DNA double-strand breaks have long been considered to be responsible for the induction of radiation induced chromosomal aberrations, the multiple steps likely to be involved are not known. Using conventional Giemsa banding as well as FISH and PCC technology, Darroudi et al. explored the modulating effects of DNA repair inhibitors on the frequency of radiation-induced dicentric and translocation chromosomes in human lymphocytes. Ara-A was found to increase the frequency of both dicentrics and translocations, whereas only dicentrics increased after treatment with 3-aminobenzamide and ara-C. The kinetics of formation of translocations after irradiation were found to be different from those of dicentric chromosomes. While DNA double-strand breaks was found to be the major lesion involved in translocation induction, dicentric chromosomes seem to be induced by other lesions as well. These results suggest that the two types of aberrations may be formed by partly different mechanisms.

Matteucci et al. (Viterbo) reported on the effect of caffeine, camptothecin (CPT) and etoposide (VP16) on the frequency of chromosomal aberrations induced by X-irradiation in the G2-phase in normal and FA lymphoblasts. FA cells of complementation group B, but not FA cell of groups A and C, showed increased sensitivity to caffeine. In contrast, FA-C cells were found to be less sensitive to camptothecin than normal cells.

In a study of the adaptive response to X-irradiation in human lymphocytes, using the frequency of micronuclei to indicate adaptation, Wojewodzka and Szumiel (Warsaw) found that three of four donors showed adaptive response. No relationship was found between the presence of an adaptive response and

DNA repair activity, measured by the 'comet' assay. However, inhibitors of cellular signal transduction such as staurosporine, TMB-8 and anti-CD38ab, were found to prevent the adaptive response, but did not affect the rate of DNA repair. These results were taken to support the hypothesis that adaptation may depend on mechanisms involved in the control of cell-cycle progression.
